I went 3-0 after drafting this sweet Blue/Green deck:

http://tappedout.net/mtg-decks/simic-midrange-2015-07-18/

P1P1: Chose a Soulblade Djinn. Was passed a Whirler Rogue, so I figured Blue was going to be open. It was.

Got 3x Rhox Maulers, passing an extra because I couldn't fit that many 5 drops in my deck.

Highlights:

Match 1: My opponent was Rakdos sacrifice. He defeated me after a protracted game 1 with that 3/3 that becomes a 5/3 first striker if it's his turn. Game 2, I got a quick ramp out and played Rhox Mauler turn 4 followed by Whirler Rogue, made Rhox unblockable, smash face. Disciple of the Ring did great work when I cast it with mana to spare, then tapped an attacker when it played the Seismic Elemental (ground creatures can't block). Totally shut him down, and I put the game away soon after. Game 3, blowout city with a Scryfish on turn 2, opponent plays Nantuko Husk, pass turn 3, block Husk after opponent plays Mage Ring Bully, disperse the husk after it sacrifices a real creature. So much tempo and card advantage. Followed up with gas for days.

Match 2: BG Elves. Game 1, both of us were out of gas, and with each of us in a land pocket. Draw Nissa's Revelation. Play it, scry 5 and put extraneous lands on the bottom. Reveal a Soulblade Djinn, draw 4 and gain 3 life. It's like I just cast Sphinx's Revelation! Drew enough gas to put the game away with a million prowess triggers.

Match 3: All Rhox Maulers, all the time. Game 1, my 6/6 serpent held off his 4/6 Sentinel of the Eternal Watch because he was forced to use the tap trigger on my renowned Rhox Maulers (naturally). We were at a board stall, and Nissa's Revelation revealed a Disciple of the Ring to break the board stall. Game 2, Nissa's Revelation into Rhox Mauler. The last play of the game was me playing Disciple of the Ring, tapping my opponent's thopter token, then beating him up with a Soulblade Djinn.

All in all, cards performed better than I expected. Disciple of the Ring is so rough when you have mana open (and sorceries/instants in the graveyard). I thought it'd be just a 3/4 do-nothing, but it did more than nothing and pulled its weight. Great stuff. Though I had great success with Nissa's Revelation, that was definitely due to having a high proportion of huge midrange threats (3x Rhox, Soulblade, Disciple). I wouldn't take a Nissa's Revelation unless you both had the threats and the ramp. I had 3 ramp spells, all were great.

Why does nature vial with itself?

Are you asking why does nature compete with itself? Well nature isn't a thing per se, its just a bunch of separate species that evolved to survive through any means even to the detriment of other species. There is no grand overarching design .
I've never seen vial used as a verb.. You should probably explain your question better.

Ah.

Well consider an environment in which there was no competition. The organisms which live in it will expand, populations with boom. Eventually, resources will become limited. When resources are limited, non-competitive organisms will cease to exist if competitive organisms beat them to the limited resources.

tl;dr natural selection
I believe that's the "point". The entire point of the Universe is "Life". Every single atom is striving to meet that goal, all the time, every time.

Not quite - life requires an enormous amount of structure and order. The universe naturally moves towards chaos. The fact that there is life is quite an anomaly which is a result of a very lucky set of circumstances which we can't even begin to evaluate.

tl;dr entropy and Newton's laws of thermodynamics

You may find this an interesting read, on that topic.

The paper in question can be found here.

Life itself is definitely not the "point" of the universe, but if the Universe really did just move towards more chaos primarily, it would have been incredibly difficult for the level of complexity required for life to evolve. There is an interesting push-and-pull balancing act between order and chaos (hilariously, this falls in line rather well with what many human religions have believed for ages).

I hope you find his theory interesting at the least, it's a rather compelling argument as far as I can see. :)

The concept of nature "vying with itself" is a false assumption based on projecting human narratives onto something that we do not understand. Reality is a complex series of shit happening, for reasons we don't know. Sometimes this shit forms patterns, which build up into bigger patterns, which start interacting with each other in various ways and building yet new patterns, until we have people sitting here and wondering about "why" it does things.

We don't know the answer, in all honesty. My personal impression? There's stuff because otherwise there would be nothing at all, and part of the nature of having stuff is all that stuff not being static, meaning it has to interact in various ways and reform itself into "new" things. (If stuff was static, we wouldn't have "stuff," we'd just have one thing, which would be for all intents and purposes pretty much the same as "nothing," as there would be no real interactions to observe and experience.)

Welcome.

This is not a clone of /r/copwatch, but something much more practical. It is a place for one thing: collections of publicly available personal information about individual police officers who have done something awful on camera.

My goal in creating and moderating this sub is to encourage meaningful opposition to violent oppression and abuse by police forces, especially in the United States of America. I don't think that just watching videos of police brutality and making angry comment threads accomplishes anything useful. I also don't think that organized protest is very effective, though it can spread awareness. I spent a long time considering what might actually get something done about this, and I concluded that one way to enable opposition would be to simply assemble a collection of verifiable, publicly available data about individual police officers and the abuses they have committed.

This resource will take a general understanding about police brutality and what it is, and turn it into a collection of specific, personally relevant details. It is one thing to watch videos of people you don't know and never will, and to read articles about societal trends and racism and other things that are really quite abstract to many readers. It is another to know that Firstname Lastname living across town kicked some poor kid's face in at a traffic stop, didn't even stand trial, and still works for your local police department. This sub is meant to take anonymous abstractions and turn them into a visceral, human reality that people can relate to their lives and communities.

What this sub is not:

  • Not for general police brutality content and discussion, which is widely available elsewhere
  • Not for encouraging or planning illegal activity, such as harassment
  • Not a place for doxxing: only publicly available information may be shared

What belongs here:

  • Meta threads about this sub and its rightful purpose (criticism and calls for change in policy are welcome)
  • Threads that aggregate public info on cops who've done awful things

Submission guideline

  • One thread per cop
  • Include a video of each known offense
  • Include any personal info that is public (often full name, badge number, headshot, and a department address)
  • Refrain from threats and other illegal behavior. Stick with the facts.
  • Title Format: (City, State) Firstname Lastname: brief, clever tagline

Thank you, and again, welcome.
